title: Behind the Runny Nose
subtitle: Many years of a blocked nose, from the first visit to the operating room
description: Classifying the rhinitis, asking about the rest of the airway, a common testing pitfall, choosing the first prescription under the 2024-2025 ARIA guidelines, explaining the spray that stopped working, and what to do when correct treatment is not enough.

steps.title: Step 1/6: How Bad, How Often
steps.scenario: A 41-year-old man comes to clinic for the first time. For many years he has had bilateral nasal obstruction, watery rhinorrhea and postnasal drip. The symptoms are there most days of the week, all year round. He says they wreck his concentration at work and wake him at night.
steps.media: Load image: Nasal endoscopy at the first visit, unannotated: pale, boggy inferior turbinates with clear watery secretion. Caption: 'First visit.'
steps.question: How do you classify his rhinitis?

options.text: (A) Intermittent, mild
(B) Intermittent, moderate to severe
(C) Persistent, moderate to severe
(D) Persistent, mild

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

ARIA classifies rhinitis on two axes. Duration: persistent means symptoms on more than 4 days a week and for more than 4 consecutive weeks; anything less is intermittent. Severity: moderate to severe means the symptoms disturb sleep, daily activities, work or school, or are simply troublesome; if none of those apply, it is mild. He has both: symptoms most days for years, and they cost him sleep and concentration.

The classification matters because it sets the starting point for treatment. Mild intermittent disease can start with an antihistamine alone. Moderate to severe disease, especially persistent, starts higher.

Why the others fail:
(A) Fails on both axes. Most days for years is not intermittent, and lost sleep is not mild.
(B) Right on severity, wrong on duration. Intermittent means 4 days a week or fewer, or 4 weeks or fewer at a time.
(D) Right on duration, wrong on severity. Symptoms that wake him at night and affect his work are moderate to severe by definition.

Keypoint: ask how many days a week, how many weeks in a row, and whether it affects sleep or work.

Reference: Bousquet J, Khaltaev N, Cruz AA, et al. Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma (ARIA) 2008 update. Allergy. 2008;63(Suppl 86):8-160. doi:10.1111/j.1398-9995.2007.01620.x.

steps.title: Step 2/6: Beyond the Nose
steps.scenario: You have classified him as persistent, moderate to severe. Before you write a prescription, there is more history to take.
steps.question: What else do you ask about at this visit?

options.text: (A) Wheeze, cough or chest tightness, and itchy or watery eyes
(B) Chronic diarrhea and abdominal bloating
(C) Headache and vertigo
(D) Joint pain and morning stiffness

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The name of the guideline is Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma. The upper and lower airway share the same lining and the same inflammation, and a large proportion of patients with allergic rhinitis also have asthma, often undiagnosed. Allergic conjunctivitis is the other common companion. Asking about chest symptoms and eye symptoms takes a minute, and the answers change what you prescribe and who else needs to see him.

Why the others fail:
(B) Gut symptoms are not part of the allergic airway. They would send you toward a different diagnosis altogether.
(C) Headache and vertigo are not comorbidities of allergic rhinitis, and asking about them here does not change management.
(D) Joint symptoms belong to a different history.

Keypoint: allergic rhinitis is one airway disease with a nose, a chest and two eyes.

Reference: Bousquet J, Khaltaev N, Cruz AA, et al. Allergy. 2008;63(Suppl 86):8-160. Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, Vieira RJ, et al. ARIA-EAACI Guidelines 2024-2025 Revision: Part I, Intranasal Treatments. Allergy. 2026;81:954-976. doi:10.1111/all.70131.

steps.title: Step 3/6: The Tablet Yesterday
steps.scenario: You recommend skin prick testing to identify his allergens. As the nurse sets up, he mentions that his nose was itchy yesterday so he took an antihistamine tablet. He asks whether that matters.
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: (A) Go ahead with the skin prick test; one tablet does not affect it
(B) Increase the allergen concentration to overcome the antihistamine
(C) Do the test today and repeat it if it comes back negative
(D) Postpone the skin test, or send serum specific IgE instead

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Antihistamines suppress the wheal and flare that the skin prick test relies on. A test done under their effect can come back negative in a patient who is clearly allergic. The controls are there to catch this: if the histamine positive control does not react, the test cannot be read. The options are to postpone until the drug has cleared, which for most modern antihistamines is a matter of days, or to send blood for serum specific IgE, which is not affected by antihistamines.

Why the others fail:
(A) One tablet is enough. Second-generation antihistamines last around a day, and some persist longer.
(B) The allergen is not the problem; the skin's ability to respond is. A stronger extract on a suppressed skin gives an unreadable result and a risk of irritant reaction.
(C) A negative test under antihistamine tells you nothing, so repeating it costs the patient a second visit for no reason. Better to do it right once.

Keypoint: check the positive control, and if the patient has taken an antihistamine, test the blood or come back another day.

Reference: Bousquet J, Khaltaev N, Cruz AA, et al. Allergy. 2008;63(Suppl 86):8-160.

steps.title: Step 4/6: The First Prescription
steps.scenario:
Serum specific IgE confirms house dust mite sensitization. He has no asthma symptoms. He is not on any medication and has never used a nasal spray properly.

Persistent, moderate to severe allergic rhinitis.
steps.question: What do you prescribe first?

options.text: (A) A second-generation oral antihistamine alone
(B) A fixed-combination intranasal antihistamine and corticosteroid spray, such as azelastine-fluticasone
(C) An intranasal corticosteroid, plus a topical decongestant for the first two weeks while it takes effect
(D) Montelukast plus an oral antihistamine

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The 2024-2025 ARIA revision changed this answer. For patients whose symptoms are unlikely to be controlled by a single agent, it gives a strong recommendation for the fixed INAH+INCS combination over no treatment, and a conditional recommendation for INAH+INCS over INCS alone, with the combination particularly favored in patients with more severe symptoms. Within the class it suggests azelastine-fluticasone over olopatadine-mometasone. The combination works faster than INCS alone, and patients using it report higher satisfaction and less need for extra medication.

An INCS alone remains a reasonable choice where cost or availability is a problem; the guideline says so explicitly. What he should not get is a plan built on oral antihistamine alone, a decongestant, or montelukast.

Why the others fail:
(A) Oral antihistamines work, and the guideline gives a strong recommendation for them over nothing. But it also gives a strong recommendation for INCS over oral antihistamines, because INCS control nasal symptoms and quality of life better. For moderate to severe persistent disease, an oral antihistamine alone is under-treatment.
(C) The guideline now suggests against adding a topical decongestant to an INCS. It adds no efficacy, adds adverse events, and adds cost. Short bridging for fewer than 5 days is the only concession, and even then INAH+INCS does the same job without the rebound risk.
(D) Montelukast has important safety concerns, and the guideline gives a strong recommendation for oral antihistamines over leukotriene antagonists, plus a conditional recommendation against adding one to the other. There is no place for it here.

Keypoint: for moderate to severe disease, start with the INAH+INCS combination; if that is not available, INCS alone.

Reference: Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, Vieira RJ, et al. ARIA-EAACI Guidelines 2024-2025 Revision: Part I, Intranasal Treatments. Allergy. 2026;81:954-976. doi:10.1111/all.70131. Vieira RJ, Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, et al. ARIA-EAACI Guidelines 2024-2025 Revision: Part II, Oral and Ocular Treatments. Allergy. 2026;81:1947-1970. doi:10.1111/all.70305.

steps.title: Step 5/6: The Spray That Stopped Working
steps.scenario: As you hand him the prescription he says: a few years ago he bought a nasal spray from the pharmacy that opened his nose within minutes. After a month of daily use it stopped working and his nose felt worse than before. He wants to know if this new spray will do the same thing.
steps.question: What do you tell him?

options.text: (A) Both are antihistamines, and any antihistamine loses effect with daily use
(B) Long-term steroid spray thins the nasal lining, so he should use the new one for no more than a week
(C) The pharmacy spray was a topical decongestant, which should not be used for more than 5 days because of rebound congestion; the new spray is different and is meant for daily long-term use
(D) The pharmacy spray was a steroid he used incorrectly, and the new one will work if he uses it properly

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

A spray that opens the nose in minutes is a topical decongestant such as oxymetazoline or xylometazoline. It constricts the vessels in the turbinates, and with continued use the vessels stop responding and then dilate harder when the drug wears off. That is rebound congestion, and after weeks of use the nose is more blocked than it started. The 2024-2025 ARIA revision now suggests against using these sprays beyond 5 days, and preferably shorter, and advises avoiding them altogether in children under 12, in pregnancy and in the elderly.

The combination spray he has been given contains an antihistamine and a corticosteroid. It does not cause rebound. It is meant to be used every day for as long as the symptoms last, and it takes days rather than minutes to reach full effect, so he should not judge it by the first dose.

Why the others fail:
(A) Decongestants are not antihistamines, and antihistamines do not lose effect with daily use.
(B) A common fear with no evidence behind it. Long-term intranasal corticosteroids have not been shown to thin or damage the nasal mucosa. Stopping after a week guarantees failure.
(D) A steroid spray does not open the nose within minutes. The speed of onset is the giveaway that it was a decongestant.

Keypoint: fast onset means decongestant; decongestants are for 5 days at most; the combination spray is for every day.

Reference: Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, Vieira RJ, et al. Allergy. 2026;81:954-976. doi:10.1111/all.70131.

steps.title: Step 6/6: Three Months Later
steps.scenario:
He returns after three months. Rhinorrhea and itch are much better. But he says the blockage is no better at all. You watch him use the spray: head neutral, nozzle angled away from the septum, gentle sniff. Technique is correct.

You perform nasal endoscopy. The septum is deviated posteriorly to the right, and both inferior turbinates are enlarged with no mucosal response to decongestant.
steps.media: Load image: Nasal endoscopy, unannotated, showing the posterior septal deviation to the right and the enlarged inferior turbinates. Caption: 'Three months later.'
steps.question: What do you recommend?

options.text: (A) Septoplasty with inferior turbinate reduction, and continue the intranasal treatment afterward
(B) Double the dose of the combination spray and review in another three months
(C) A short course of oral corticosteroid to break the cycle
(D) Surgery, after which the allergy treatment can stop

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The medication has done what medication can do: the itch and the running have settled. What is left is a fixed obstruction that no spray will change. A deviated septum is bone and cartilage. Inferior turbinates that do not shrink with a decongestant have submucosal hypertrophy rather than reversible swelling. Both are surgical problems. Septoplasty and turbinate reduction relieve the obstruction and, by opening the nose, also let the spray reach the mucosa it is meant to treat.

The operation does not remove the allergy. He still has house dust mite sensitization and he will still have inflammation. The spray continues after surgery.

One thing to check before any of this: technique. The ARIA guidelines assume correct use of intranasal sprays, and poor technique is a common reason for apparent failure. Here you watched him and it was fine, which is why the next step is endoscopy rather than another round of coaching.

Why the others fail:
(B) More of the same drug will not move a deviated septum. Three more months is three months of a blocked nose for nothing.
(C) Oral steroids may briefly shrink mucosa, but they do nothing for the septum, the turbinates return as soon as the course ends, and repeated courses carry real harm.
(D) Surgery corrects the anatomy, not the immunology. Stopping the spray afterward brings back the rhinorrhea and itch that it had controlled.

Keypoint: when the itch and the running are controlled but the blockage is not, look inside; medication does not treat anatomy.

Reference: Bousquet J, Khaltaev N, Cruz AA, et al. Allergy. 2008;63(Suppl 86):8-160. Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, Vieira RJ, et al. Allergy. 2026;81:954-976. doi:10.1111/all.70131.
